# Linear cap stability and an enclosing triangle for near-triangle quadrilaterals

This is an ordinary planar theorem. It controls the ENTIRE missing mass
of one explicit circumscribed triangle by maximal-depth excess; the
missing part need not be confined to a small vertex neighborhood.
It consequently extends the corner-localized result to every convex
quadrilateral in an explicit affine neighborhood of a triangle.

Let Gamma=4/9 and let D(Q) denote normalized ordinary maximal halfspace
depth. If a full-dimensional convex quadrilateral Q admits an invertible
affine map A such that

    dist_H,infinity(AQ,T)<=1/240000,
    T=conv(0,e_1,e_2),

then there is a full-dimensional triangle S containing Q with

    tau=1-|Q|/|S| <=45[D(Q)-Gamma],
    dist_cap(mu_Q,mu_S)=tau.                            (1)

In particular

    D(Q)-Gamma >=(1/45) inf_(affine triangles S')
                                    dist_cap(mu_Q,mu_(S')).

The existence of the initial affine map is the stated local hypothesis.
No closest triangle, minimum circumscribed-area triangle, or minimizing
affine map is assumed to exist. The proof selects vertices and constructs
S directly. No analogous claim about general pentagons or smooth bodies
is made.

## 1. An explicit outer comparison for a small quadrilateral bump

First suppose

    Q=conv(0,e_1,e_2,p),  p=(1+h-k,k),
    0<h<=1/10000, 0<k<1+h.

Exchanging e_1 and e_2 if necessary makes k<= (1+h)/2. In particular
k<1. Put

    b=1+h/(1-k), S=conv(0,b e_1,e_2).

This triangle contains Q. Its missing part is the corner triangle at
b e_1 cut off by the line through e_1 and p. Its relative area and its
two incident-edge cut fractions are

    tau=hk/(1+h-k),
    r_1=h/(1+h-k), r_2=k,  tau=r_1 r_2.               (2)

The labeling ensures

    0<tau<=h<=1/10000,
    r_1<=2h/(1+h)<1/100,
    r_2<51/100.                                      (3)

Map S affinely to a standard triangle and call its removed vertex 0,
its short-cut-edge endpoint 1 and its long-cut-edge endpoint 2. In
barycentric coordinates, the removed triangle R has the description

    u=lambda_1>=0, v=lambda_2>=0,
    u/r_1+v/r_2<=1, lambda_0=1-u-v.                   (4)

Its area is tau|S|. Since R is a halfspace trace of S disjoint from Q
except for its boundary, normalized uniform measures satisfy

    dist_cap(mu_Q,mu_S)=TV(mu_Q,mu_S)=tau.              (5)

The first equality is witnessed by that removed-corner halfspace; the
second is the exact nested-body TV identity. The edge fraction r_2 may
stay close to one half while tau tends to zero. Thus the previous
small-vertex-neighborhood theorem does not by itself cover this regime.

## 2. Explicit control of every low-volume triangle cap

Set zeta=kappa=1/10000 and write beta=1/3. Suppose a point y has all
three barycentric coordinates in [beta-zeta,beta+zeta]. A through-y
cap of S whose area fraction is at most Gamma+kappa must isolate one
vertex. For that vertex i it can be written

    a_j lambda_j(x)+a_k lambda_k(x)<=1,
    a_j lambda_j(y)+a_k lambda_k(y)=1,
    29/20 < a_j,a_k <31/20.                           (6)

Here j,k are the other two indices. All statements concern the SAME
actual cap; no separate normal is chosen for different source pieces.

First consider a cap containing two vertices. Its complement isolates
the third. If the complementary edge intercepts are t_j,t_k, its area
fraction is t_j t_k, with lambda_j(y)/t_j+lambda_k(y)/t_k=1 and
0<t_j,t_k<=1. Setting x=lambda_j(y)/t_j restricts x to
[lambda_j(y),1-lambda_k(y)]. The maximum of
lambda_j(y)lambda_k(y)/[x(1-x)] occurs at an endpoint. It is at most
max{lambda_j/(1-lambda_k),lambda_k/(1-lambda_j)}. Since all coordinates
are below 17/50, this is at most 17/33. The original cap consequently
has fraction at least 16/33>Gamma+kappa. This excludes two-vertex caps.

For a one-vertex cap, the coefficients are greater than one and its area
fraction is 1/(a_j a_k). Hence a low-volume cap has

    a_j+a_k <=30000/9997=:U,
    a_j a_k >=90000/40009=:P.

If one coefficient were at most 29/20, the product would be at most
(29/20)(U-29/20), since x(U-x) increases up to U/2. If one were at least
31/20, the product would be at most (31/20)(U-31/20), since that function
decreases beyond U/2. Both possibilities contradict the exact gaps

    P-(29/20)(U-29/20)=110147293/159987989200>0,
    P-(31/20)(U-31/20)= 95744053/159987989200>0.

This proves (6). Cuts through a vertex are covered by approximation
with through-y generic cuts and continuity of area. Thus no closed
boundary direction is omitted from the conclusion.

## 3. Exact partial-removal bounds and an actual point

Use the point y with barycentrics

    lambda_0=1/3-9tau/20,
    lambda_1=1/3+3tau/10,
    lambda_2=1/3+3tau/20.                              (7)

By (3) these lie in the window used in Section 2. The point is interior
to Q: all its coordinates are positive and lambda_1>r_1, so it lies
strictly outside the removed corner (4).

For a low-volume cap at vertex 0, the loss is at most tau|S|. For a
low-volume cap at vertex 1, the loss is zero. Indeed (4) gives u<=1/100,
and (6) implies

    a_0 lambda_0+a_2 lambda_2
       >=(29/20)(1-u)>1

on R, excluding every removed point from that cap.

For a low-volume cap at vertex 2, its inequality on R implies

    v>=1-1/a_0+(a_1/a_0-1)u
      >=9/29-1/1550 >3/10.

The last strict gap is 218/22475. In the triangle (4), the fraction
with v>=3/10 is (1-(3/10)/r_2)_+^2. Since r_2<=51/100, it is at most
49/289<1/5. Thus this cap loses at most (tau/5)|S|. We have established
the simultaneous removal bounds

    (tau, 0, tau/5)|S|                               (8)

for the three possible low-cap types.

Every one-vertex cap through y in S has fraction at least four times
the product of the other two barycentric coordinates, by AM--GM on
its two edge-intercept parameters. Combining this with (7)-(8), the
three resulting lower bounds for its actual Q mass, divided by |S|,
are respectively

    Gamma-2tau/5+9tau^2/50,
    Gamma-2tau/5-27tau^2/100,
    Gamma-2tau/5-27tau^2/50.                           (9)

Every remaining through-y cap has S fraction greater than Gamma+kappa.
Deleting at most tau<=kappa leaves at least Gamma|S|, which is larger
than the smallest expression in (9). Hence ALL through-y caps of Q,
and therefore all containing halfspaces, have normalized mass at least

    [Gamma-2tau/5-27tau^2/50]/(1-tau).

It follows that

    D(Q)-Gamma >=[2tau/45-27tau^2/50]/(1-tau)
                >=tau/45.                            (10)

The final comparison has exact numerator tau(10-233tau)/450 after
subtracting tau/45; it holds for tau<=10/233, in particular throughout
(3). This proves an actual center lower bound and the total missing-mass
control (1) for the normalized bump family, using every direction.

## 4. Every sufficiently near-triangle quadrilateral has this form

It remains to derive the small-h representation from the stated metric
hypothesis. Work in an affine frame with dist_H,infinity(Q,T)<=delta,
where delta<=1/240000. Then every Q point satisfies

    x_1,x_2>=-delta, x_1+x_2<=1+2delta,
    x_1,x_2<=1+delta.

Choose a Q vertex p_1 maximizing x_1, a vertex p_2 maximizing x_2, and
a vertex p_0 minimizing x_1+x_2. Hausdorff approximation to e_1,e_2,0
gives respectively x_1(p_1)>=1-delta, x_2(p_2)>=1-delta and
x_1(p_0)+x_2(p_0)<=2delta. The preceding coordinate bounds imply

    ||p_i-e_i||_infinity<=3delta, i=1,2,
    ||p_0||_infinity<=3delta.

These are three distinct vertices. The determinant of p_1-p_0,p_2-p_0
is at least (1-6delta)^2-(6delta)^2=1-12delta. Their inscribed triangle
T_in therefore has area at least (1-12delta)/2. Meanwhile Q lies in
the triangle {x_i>=-delta, sum x_i<=1+2delta}, whose area is
(1+4delta)^2/2. Consequently

    h=|Q|/|T_in|-1
       <=(20delta+16delta^2)/(1-12delta)
       <=24delta<=1/10000.                            (11)

No optimization or attainment of an inscribed triangle was required.
Because Q has exactly four vertices, its fourth vertex lies outside
exactly one edge of T_in and inside the supporting halfplanes of its
other two edges. Relabel the triangle so that the former edge joins
e_1,e_2 after an affine map, while the opposite vertex is zero. The
fourth vertex then has positive coordinates of sum 1+h, giving exactly
p=(1+h-k,k), with 0<k<1+h. Its positivity follows because all four
polygon vertices are extreme; collinear redundant points may simply be
discarded, reducing the body to a triangle. Exchanging the two edge
endpoints gives the labeling used in Section 1.

The explicit triangle S constructed there, transported back by the
composed affine map, is the single comparison required in (1). Ordinary
depth and halfspace-cap distance are invariant under this affine map.
This completes the theorem and proves that the near-triangle hypothesis
does not conceal a chosen Euclidean encoding of all quadrilaterals.

## 5. Scope

The controlled residual is the TOTAL relative area of S outside Q. In
particular its portion outside any fixed vertex neighborhoods is also
at most 45[D(Q)-4/9]. The residual can extend halfway along a side of S,
so this is stronger than the previous localized-corner theorem.
The proof does not claim S minimizes area or cap distance. It does not
extend to an arbitrary number of polygon vertices without an additional
argument handling coupled cuts of more than one corner or facet.

The exact verifier is
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_near_triangle_quadrilateral_cap_stability.py`.
It passes 8847 rational checks, including the displayed constants,
enclosing-triangle and cut-area identities, 224 through-point directions
for each of 28 quadrilaterals, and the metric-to-area normalization.
Those finite directional checks supplement the all-direction proof in
Sections 2--3; they do not supply its quantifier.
